preamble: The near-close back rounded vowel [ʊ] is unrounded and lowered to the open-mid back unrounded vowel [ʌ]. This is the FOOT–STRUT split of Early Modern English, first clearly described in 1644: Middle English short /u/ had first been laxed to [ʊ] (u → ʊ), and this [ʊ] then unrounded in cut, dull, fun. Unrounding was blocked mainly after labial consonants and before /l ʃ tʃ/, leaving put, pull, full with [ʊ] beside putt, cut, dull with [ʌ]. Most of Northern England and the English Midlands did not undergo the change and keep [ʊ] (dull /dʊl/, fun /fʊn/).

examples.from: Early Modern English cut, lax [ʊ] (< Middle English /u/)
examples.note: Unrounded and lowered in the STRUT lexical set; Wells (1982) reconstructs a transitional unrounded [ɤ] between the two stages.
Words with a preceding labial (put, pull, full) kept the rounded vowel, splitting the phoneme into FOOT /ʊ/ and STRUT /ʌ/; Northern England keeps /fʊn/.

sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511611759
